title: Native Nations and Traditional Knowledge
description: Ten texts on Native nations today and in history: the Three Sisters garden, a Navajo weaver, the Ojibwe wild-rice harvest, a language program, Haudenosaunee consensus, a powwow, cultural burning, a tribal college, a returned Haida treasure and Indigenous teachers in Morocco.
topic: Native peoples, their knowledge and their communities

lessons.title: The Three Sisters
lessons.summary: A Seneca gardener explains how corn, beans and squash grow together.
lessons.text:
Every spring, Rena Hill plants a garden behind the community center on the Seneca territory where she grew up. It is not a garden of neat rows. Instead, it is a field of low, round hills of earth, and in each hill Rena plants three crops together: corn, beans and squash. In Haudenosaunee tradition, these crops are known as the Three Sisters, and they have been grown together here for centuries.

The planting follows a strict order. First, when the soil has warmed, Rena puts a few corn seeds in the top of each hill. If she plants too early, the seeds lie in cold, wet ground and turn rotten before they can grow. About two weeks later, when the corn is about as tall as her hand, she plants beans around it, and soon after that, squash between the hills.

Each sister has her own job. The corn grows tall and straight, and the beans climb it as if it were a pole. The beans, in turn, feed the soil: tiny living things on their roots take nitrogen, a gas, from the air and leave it in the earth, where the corn can use it. The squash spreads its wide leaves over the ground, keeping the soil cool and moist and leaving little room for weeds.

Scientists describe this as an ecological system, in which each part supports the others. Rena points out, however, that the women who devised it did not need the word. Haudenosaunee women, who were traditionally responsible for the fields, devised the method through careful observation and passed it on from mother to daughter. Together, the three crops also make a balanced diet: corn gives energy, beans give protein, and squash gives vitamins.

The ecological benefits are not only a matter of history. Many modern farms show a heavy reliance on chemical fertilizer, which can wash into rivers and lakes. A Three Sisters garden needs far less, because the beans do much of that work. Rena's own reliance is on the plants themselves.

Not everything goes well, of course. In a wet August, a white fungus sometimes appears on the squash leaves, like a fine powder. Rena removes the worst leaves and gives the plants more space, so that air can move between them. Alternatively, she sprays the plants with a mix of milk and water, an old garden remedy. Alternatively, in a very bad year, she simply waits for a dry week. The fungus rarely kills the plants.

In September, the garden's volunteers hold a harvest meal. People bring homemade corn soup, homemade bread and jars of homemade strawberry jelly. The children spread the jelly on the bread. Before everyone eats, Rena thanks the Three Sisters, and she saves the best seeds for next spring.

Questions:
Why does Rena wait for the soil to warm before she plants corn?
If she plants too early, the seeds lie in cold, wet ground and turn rotten.
How do the beans help the corn?
They take nitrogen from the air and leave it in the soil, where the corn can use it.
Who devised the Three Sisters method?
Haudenosaunee women devised it through careful observation and passed it on to their daughters.
What does Rena do when a fungus appears on the squash leaves?
She removes the worst leaves or, alternatively, sprays the plants with milk and water.
What do people bring to the harvest meal?
They bring homemade corn soup, homemade bread and homemade strawberry jelly.

lessons.title: The Weaver at the Loom
lessons.summary: A profile of a Navajo weaver who raises her own sheep and weaves rugs from memory.
lessons.text:
Lena Begay was 8 years old when her grandmother first sat her down in front of a loom. Today, at 64, Lena is one of the most respected weavers in her part of the Navajo Nation, and her rugs hang in homes and museums across the country. Yet when visitors ask her what she does, she answers simply: "I weave, the way my grandmother wove."

Her work begins long before she sits at the loom. Lena and her husband, Ben, keep a small herd of Churro sheep, a breed that Diné families have raised for centuries. The Churro has a double coat: a soft layer close to the skin and a long, hairy outer layer that sheds rain and snow. Visitors who expect a round white sheep are often surprised by how hairy the animals look. Yet that hairy coat gives a strong, shining thread that lasts for generations.

After the sheep are sheared, Lena cleans the wool, combs it and spins it into thread by hand. Some of it she leaves in its natural shades of white, gray, brown and black. The rest she colors with plants that she gathers in the hills. She boils the plants in a large pot and lowers the wool into it. The longer the wool stays in the pot, the more the color will intensify, so a pale yellow can become a deep gold overnight. Each time she dips the wool again, the color will intensify a little more.

Her family's recipes for color are not exactly proprietary, she says, since nobody can own a plant. Still, she is discreet about them. In her view, knowledge is a gift for people who will use it well, and she shares it only with her daughters and her students. In a world where so much knowledge is proprietary, bought and sold, Lena prefers to be discreet and generous at the same time.

When she was eighteen, she sold her first rug at a trading post, and at eighteen she also decided that weaving would be her life's work. Years later, when she wanted to weave larger rugs, Ben agreed to enlarge it, and later he had to enlarge it a second time, until it filled one wall of her workshop.

Lena does not draw her designs on paper. She keeps the whole pattern in her mind and lets it grow line by line, from the bottom of the loom to the top. A large rug can take her six months or more.

Her patience has been recognized. On a shelf in her living room stands a row of awards from art markets, among them a plaque for the best weaving of the year. Lena dusts the plaque now and then, but she does not seem to think about it much. The award that matters, she says, is a young weaver finishing her first rug.

Questions:
What kind of coat does a Churro sheep have?
It has a soft layer close to the skin and a long, hairy outer layer that sheds rain and snow.
How does Lena make a color intensify?
She leaves the wool in the pot longer, so the color becomes deeper.
Why is Lena discreet about her family's recipes?
She believes knowledge is a gift for people who will use it well.
What happened when Lena was eighteen?
She sold her first rug and decided that weaving would be her life's work.
Why did Ben enlarge the loom?
Lena wanted to weave larger rugs.

lessons.title: Ricing Season
lessons.summary: An Ojibwe grandfather takes his granddaughter to harvest wild rice for the first time.
lessons.text:
Every year in late August, the wild rice on the lakes of northern Minnesota turns from green to gold. Ray Morrison is Ojibwe, and he has harvested wild rice, which the Ojibwe call manoomin, every year of his life. Last year, for the first time, his granddaughter Kayla, who was 16, came with him.

Kayla was reluctant at first. She had planned to spend the weekend with her friends, and a day on a lake did not sound exciting. However, her grandfather's enthusiasm was infectious. When he talked about ricing, his eyes shone, and his laughter was just as infectious. By the end of dinner, Kayla found herself asking questions.

For the Ojibwe, wild rice is far more than a crop. According to tradition, their ancestors traveled west for generations until they reached the place where food grows on the water. In hard winters in the past, a store of rice meant that a family would not starve. "A family with rice in the house," Ray said, "will never starve."

The harvest follows careful rules. There are dozens of rice lakes in the vicinity of the reservation. On many of them, a tribal committee decides when the rice is ready. Ricers also take only part of the crop. Some rice always falls into the water, and that, Ray explained, is not a loss but a precaution: those grains sink into the mud and become next year's plants. A life jacket is another precaution, and Ray made Kayla wear hers all day.

On the morning of the harvest, Ray stood at the back of the boat with a long pole and pushed it slowly through the tall plants. Kayla sat in front with two light sticks made of cedar. With one cedar stick, she bent the plants over the boat; with the other, she tapped them gently, so that the ready grains fell inside. Around noon, they saw an otter with two pups at the edge of the rice. The pups dove and played in the water.

Ray told her that in some years, prolonged rain in early summer raises the water so high that the young plants drown, and a whole lake produces almost nothing. A prolonged dry period can harm the rice as well.

By evening, the boat was half full, and Kayla's arms ached. "Tuckered out?" her grandfather asked. She admitted that she was completely tuckered out.

The next day, they dried the rice in the sun and then roasted it in a large metal drum over a fire. Kayla turned the drum with a crank for an hour while Ray watched the color of the grains. Turning the crank, she finally understood why her grandfather's arms were so strong.

Questions:
Why did Kayla, who was reluctant at first, agree to go ricing?
Her grandfather's enthusiasm and laughter were infectious.
Why did wild rice matter so much in hard winters?
A store of rice meant that a family would not starve.
Why is the rice that falls into the water not a loss?
It is a precaution, because those grains become next year's plants.
What did Kayla and Ray see in the vicinity of the boat around noon?
They saw an otter with two pups at the edge of the rice.
What did Kayla use to harvest the rice?
She used two light sticks made of cedar.
What can prolonged rain in early summer do?
It can raise the water so high that the young plants drown.

lessons.title: A Movie in Our Language
lessons.summary: A language program dubs a children's film into its tribal language.
lessons.text:
When Joyce Bird took over the language program in her community, only about 40 people had grown up speaking the language, and most of them were over 70. The reason was no secret. From the late nineteenth century, many Native children in the United States were sent to government boarding schools, often far from home, where they were punished for speaking their own languages. For many families, the removal of their children felt like kidnapping. Joyce's grandmother, who was taken from home at 7, always called it a kidnapping, and she spoke her language only in whispers for the rest of her life.

Joyce's program teaches the language to children after school. For years, it was paid for by a government grant, but last spring the grant expired. With the grant expired, Joyce had to find money elsewhere, so she began fundraising. There were bake sales, a dinner and a letter to every family in the community. The fundraising went better than she had dared to hope.

She also wanted to try something new. She had read that Bambi was dubbed into Arapaho in 1994 and that Star Wars was dubbed into Navajo in 2013, and that children who would never sit through a grammar lesson watched these films again and again. Why not have a movie dubbed into their own language?

The first problem was choosing the movie, and it turned into a real dilemma. The teenagers on the committee wanted an old gangster movie, full of fast cars and tough talk. The elders wanted a film that a grandmother could watch with a child of 5. In the end, one elder solved the dilemma by pointing out that a gangster movie would need dozens of words the language had never had. Everyone laughed, and they chose a cartoon about a family of bears.

The second problem was the rights. Joyce wrote to the studio that owned the film, expecting a polite refusal. Instead, she reached a manager who was sympathetic to the idea. Her own grandparents, the manager said, had lost their language when they moved to a new country. With such a sympathetic partner, the rights were settled within a month.

Someone suggested using automation, computer programs that can turn written words into speech. Joyce refused. Automation might work for large languages, she said, but no machine had learned theirs, and the whole point was to hear real voices. So elders recorded the parts of the adult bears, and children from the program recorded the young ones.

At the first showing, in the school gym, nobody worried about a spoiler. Most families had seen the film in English, so there was no spoiler to give away. Yet when the mother bear spoke her first line in their language, the gym went silent, and then people cheered. For Joyce, the moment seemed to validate years of work. For the elders, it seemed to validate something deeper: their language belonged on a screen as much as any other.

Questions:
Why did Joyce begin fundraising?
The government grant that paid for the program had expired.
What did Joyce's grandmother call her removal to a boarding school?
She always called it a kidnapping.
What was the committee's dilemma?
The teenagers wanted a gangster movie, but the elders wanted a film for small children.
Why did Joyce refuse to use automation?
No machine had learned their language, and she wanted people to hear real voices.
Why did nobody worry about a spoiler?
Most families had already seen the film in English.

lessons.title: Across the Fire
lessons.summary: An essay on how the Haudenosaunee reach decisions by consensus.
lessons.text:
Most of us learn in school that democracy means voting: the side with more votes wins. It is a useful idea, but not the only one. For centuries, the Haudenosaunee, the six nations long called the Iroquois by outsiders, have practiced a different conception of how a people should decide.

The Haudenosaunee alliance unites the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora nations under the Great Law of Peace. In its conception, a decision is not a contest to be won. It is a shared mind to be reached.

A question brought before the Grand Council is discussed first by one group of nations, then passed "across the fire" to another group, and finally to the Onondaga, who keep the council fire. At each stage, a speaker carefully summarizes what has been said, so that everyone can hear that their views were understood. Only when all the views are aligned is a decision made. If they cannot be aligned, the matter may be set aside for another day.

To an outsider, this can look slow, even like a tactic for delay. It is not meant as a tactic at all. The aim is not to defeat an opponent but to find the place where everyone's interests align. When interests align, the decision belongs to all. Speakers are expected to address ideas, not people. To denounce a rival in council would betray the very spirit the council exists to protect.

There is a good reason for such patience. A decision reached by consensus is harder to reach, but also harder to break, because nobody walks away defeated.

The same spirit shaped Haudenosaunee agreements with Europeans. The Two Row belt, made of white shell beads with two parallel purple rows, is said to record an agreement with Dutch traders in 1613: two boats traveling side by side down the same river, neither trying to steer the other. Later, the Haudenosaunee and the British described their alliance as a Covenant Chain, which had to be polished at regular meetings so that it would not rust. Such a covenant was meant to last as long as the grass is green and the rivers flow, in other words, for eternity. Yet even a promise made for eternity, the Haudenosaunee believed, must be renewed by each generation.

Outsiders have often found their own ideas in the Haudenosaunee. Some argue that the alliance influenced the authors of the United States Constitution, and in 1988 Congress formally recognized that influence. Friedrich Engels, drawing on an American scholar's studies, saw in it an early form of communism. Each viewpoint says as much about the viewer as about the Haudenosaunee. The Haudenosaunee themselves never set out to prove anything about democracy or communism. Their own viewpoint is simpler: a people should keep talking until it can move forward together.

Questions:
What happens at each stage of a discussion in the Grand Council?
A speaker summarizes what has been said, so that everyone knows their views were understood.
When is a decision made?
A decision is made only when all the views are aligned.
Why is it wrong to denounce a rival in council?
Speakers are expected to address ideas, not people.
What does the Two Row belt show?
It shows two boats traveling side by side, neither trying to steer the other.
How long was the Covenant Chain meant to last?
It was meant to last for eternity, but each generation had to renew it.

lessons.title: A Visitor's Guide to the Powwow
lessons.summary: A powwow committee explains to first-time visitors what to expect and how to behave.
lessons.text:
Every summer, our community holds a three-day powwow on the field behind the school, and every summer we welcome hundreds of visitors who have never been to one. This guide is for you.

A powwow is a social gathering of song and dance. It is not a show put on for tourists, but it is open to everyone, whatever your ethnicity. Nobody at the gate will ask about your ethnicity or your background. The dancers come from many nations, and some of them travel thousands of miles to be here.

Arrive early. One perk of arriving early is a parking space close to the arena. Another perk is the chance to watch the dancers getting ready and to find a good place to sit. Bring folding chairs: the benches closest to the arena are kept for dancers and their families.

The Grand Entry begins at noon. Veterans carry the flags into the arena, and the dancers follow in order, group after group. Please stand and remove your hat during the Grand Entry and during any song that the announcer calls an honor song. The announcer keeps the program moving, explains each dance and tells a great many jokes. You will soon find yourself chuckling, because many of the jokes are at his own expense. Even the dancers chuckle as they wait for their turn.

What the dancers wear is called regalia, not a costume. Each outfit is colorful and personal, often made by hand over many months and decorated with beads, ribbons and feathers. Many pieces are gifts from relatives, and some have deep meaning. Admire the colorful designs, but never touch a dancer's regalia, and always ask before you take a photograph. For the same reason, please understand why many Native people object to Halloween costumes with feathered headbands and braided wigs. A cheap wig and a plastic feather turn a living tradition into a joke.

Between the dances, visit the craft booths. Local artists sell jewelry, baskets, colorful blankets and smaller gifts, such as beaded coasters. A set of coasters is easy to carry home, and every purchase supports an artist. At lunchtime, food vendors hustle to serve long lines of hungry people, and the whole field is full of the hustle of a busy market.

A powwow is a long day for small children. Bring water, snacks and hats, and expect them to whine a little by late afternoon. Every parent at the powwow knows the sound, so do not worry if your child starts to whine. Nobody will mind.

Finally, listen for the announcer to invite everyone into the arena for a dance that is open to all. Visitors are welcome to join, and you do not need to know the steps. Just follow the people in front of you, move with the drum and enjoy yourself.

Questions:
Who may come to the powwow?
Everyone may come, whatever their ethnicity or background.
What is one perk of arriving early?
One perk is a parking space close to the arena.
What should visitors do during an honor song?
They should stand and remove their hats.
Why should visitors never wear a costume with a braided wig?
A cheap wig and a plastic feather turn a living tradition into a joke.
What can visitors buy at the craft booths?
They can buy jewelry, baskets, colorful blankets and beaded coasters.

lessons.title: Good Fire
lessons.summary: The Karuk Tribe in California brings back controlled burning to care for the land.
lessons.text:
Every fall, on the steep hills above the Klamath River in northern California, members of the Karuk Tribe set small fires on purpose. To a visitor, the sight can be alarming: low flames moving through the grass under the oaks, and smoke rising into the sky. However, these fires are carefully planned. For thousands of years, the Karuk and nearby nations used fire to care for the land, and today they are bringing that practice back.

Cultural burning, as it is often called, has many purposes. A low, cool fire purges the forest floor of dead branches and dry brush that would otherwise pile up year after year. Each burn purges the ground of old fuel and makes room for new growth, including the young shoots that Karuk weavers use for baskets. Fire also reduces pests. Ticks, small parasites that feed on the blood of deer and people, are far fewer after a burn, and fire also controls mistletoe, a plant parasite that lives on trees and slowly weakens them.

For about a century, this knowledge was pushed aside. In 1850, a California law made it a crime for Native people to set fire to grassland, and later, government agencies tried to put out every fire as quickly as possible. Some people who continued to burn were detained or fined. Elders still remember relatives who were detained for doing what their families had always done.

The result of a century without fire is a forest full of fuel. When a fire does start, it can grow into an enormous blaze that no forest can survive. Smoke from such fires travels hundreds of miles. In recent summers, cities across the West have woken to filthy orange skies and air so filthy that people were told to stay indoors. Doctors warn that the smoke causes serious respiratory problems, especially for children, older people and anyone with a respiratory illness. Meanwhile, many new suburbs have been built right at the edge of the forest, so that a single fire can threaten a whole suburb within hours.

Controlled burns produce smoke too, and the smell of it can make your clothes stink. "My clothes stink for days afterward," one young Karuk firefighter said, "but it's a good smell." The burns are planned for days when the wind carries the smoke away from towns, and they release far less carbon dioxide than a great blaze. Because fewer large trees are lost, more carbon stays in the forest instead of entering the air as carbon dioxide.

The Karuk are not alone. In Australia, Aboriginal communities have long practiced what is often called cool burning, and Aboriginal rangers now work with government fire services to bring it back across the country. Their message is the same as the Karuk's: fire is not only an enemy. Used with knowledge, it is also a tool.

Questions:
What does a low, cool fire do to the forest floor?
It purges the forest floor of dead branches and dry brush.
Which parasites become fewer after a burn?
Ticks and mistletoe become fewer.
What happened to some people who continued to burn after 1850?
Some of them were detained or fined.
Why is wildfire smoke dangerous?
It causes serious respiratory problems, especially for children and older people.
Why is a suburb at the edge of the forest in danger?
A single fire can reach a whole suburb within hours.
Where else do communities practice cool burning?
Aboriginal communities in Australia practice it.

lessons.title: Orientation Day
lessons.summary: A student leads new students on a tour of her tribal college in southern Arizona.
lessons.text:
On the first morning of the fall semester, Danielle Lopez led a group of new students around the tribal college where she had studied for two years. Danielle is Tohono O'odham, and the college stands on her nation's land in southern Arizona. The first tribal college opened on the Navajo Nation in 1968. Today there are more than 30 across the United States. They teach the same subjects as any other college, but they also teach the languages, history and values of the nations they serve.

The tour began in the main building, an old school that the college had decided to renovate rather than tear down. "It took three years to renovate," Danielle said, "and now the college wants to renovate the old gym too."

Their first stop was a math classroom. "Many of us are afraid of algebra," Danielle told the group. "I failed algebra twice in high school. Here, the tutors stayed with me until it made sense." A few students looked relieved.

Next, they visited the workshop where future mechanics train. Every car on the reservation eventually needs a mechanic. The instructor, whose hands were black with grease, explained that a good mechanic must understand computers as well as engines. The room smelled of oil and grease.

In the business office, Danielle showed them where she worked part-time, in payroll. "Payroll means making sure that every worker at the college is paid correctly and on time," she said. "Nobody notices payroll until something goes wrong."

Upstairs, a class on tribal government was discussing sovereignty: the right of a tribe to govern itself. That morning's topic was taxation. Like states, tribes may raise money through taxation, for example on sales on tribal land, but the rules are complex. "Taxation sounds boring," Danielle whispered, "but it's how a nation pays for its schools."

In the history classroom, students were studying the Pueblo uprising of 1680, when Pueblo nations in what is now New Mexico united and drove Spanish rulers out of their land for 12 years. The teacher called it one of the most successful uprisings in the history of the continent.

From the music room came the sound of a violin. An elder was teaching waila, the Tohono O'odham dance music that was first played on the violin and guitar. Danielle's grandfather had played the violin at every family wedding.

The last stop was the health sciences building. There, students in a public health program were studying obesity and diabetes, which affect communities across the country. Their project brings traditional desert foods back into school lunches as one way to fight obesity.

At the end of the tour, a young man asked Danielle what she liked most about the college. "Here," she said, "nobody has to choose between a degree and who they are."

Questions:
What did the college do with the old school building?
It decided to renovate the building rather than tear it down.
Why did Danielle tell the group about algebra?
She had failed algebra twice in high school, and the tutors helped her until it made sense.
What is Danielle's job at the college?
She works part-time in payroll, making sure every worker is paid correctly and on time.
What happened in the Pueblo uprising of 1680?
Pueblo nations united and drove Spanish rulers out of their land for 12 years.
What were the health students studying?
They were studying obesity and diabetes and bringing traditional foods back into school lunches.

lessons.title: A Box Comes Home
lessons.summary: An English duchess returns two Haida treasures that left their islands more than a century ago.
lessons.text:
Last spring, Lucy Williams and her nephew Owen, members of the Haida Nation's repatriation committee, flew from Haida Gwaii, a group of islands off the coast of British Columbia, to a country house in the south of England. They had come to collect two objects, a painted cedar box and a woven hat, which had left their islands more than a century earlier.

The objects belonged to the family of a duchess. While sorting an attic, the duchess had found them in a trunk, together with the household registry from 1885. The registry recorded both objects in a single line, as things bought on the Pacific coast by her great-great-grandfather. She had written to the Haida Nation herself and offered to return them. Lucy knew that the duchess's letter had been decisive. Without that decisive step, the box and the hat might have stayed in the attic for another hundred years.

Before the meeting, a guide showed the visitors around the house. It was built of golden stone from a quarry on the estate. In the old quarry, the guide explained, workers once split the stone by hammering iron wedges into a line of small holes until the rock broke apart. A rusty wedge was still kept in a glass case. Behind the stables stood the estate's old brewery, where beer had once been made for the servants. The brewery was now a tea room.

In the long hall stood a blue and white Ming vase, made in China during the Ming dynasty. On the opposite wall hung a row of old arrows. Archery had once been a fashionable sport among wealthy English families, the guide said, and the estate had employed its own fletcher, a craftsman who made arrows. The common family name Fletcher comes from that trade.

At last, they met the duchess, a warm and direct woman in her seventies. On a table in the library lay the box. It had been made from a single board of cedar, steamed and bent into four sides, and its painted faces were still bright. Owen, who is a carver himself, studied it for a long time. "Work of this caliber," he said quietly, "takes a lifetime to learn." The hat, woven from fine roots, was of the same high caliber.

"My family has cherished these things in our own way," the duchess said. "But they were never ours to cherish." Lucy thanked her and promised that the box and the hat would be cherished at home, where children could see them and carvers could learn from them.

A week later, the objects arrived on Haida Gwaii, and the community welcomed them with a feast.

Questions:
What did the household registry record?
It recorded both objects as things bought on the Pacific coast by the duchess's great-great-grandfather.
Why was the duchess's letter decisive?
Without it, the objects might have stayed in the attic for another hundred years.
How did workers split the stone in the quarry?
They hammered iron wedges into a line of small holes until the rock broke apart.
What was a fletcher?
A fletcher was a craftsman who made arrows.
What did Owen say about the box?
He said that work of this caliber takes a lifetime to learn.

lessons.title: Messages from Morocco
lessons.summary: A Navajo language teacher sends home messages from a teachers' exchange in Morocco.
lessons.text:
Sharon Yazzie teaches the Navajo language at a school in Arizona. Last spring, she spent two weeks in Morocco with a group of teachers of Native languages from the United States and Canada. They had been invited to meet teachers of Tamazight, the language of the Amazigh people of North Africa. Every evening, Sharon sent a message to her husband and their son, Tyler.

Day 1: We landed in Rabat this morning, but my luggage did not. The airline says my luggage is still in Paris and will arrive tomorrow. Luckily, I packed a toothbrush in my handbag. Morocco is beautiful already.

Day 2: My luggage arrived! Today we visited a school. In 2011, Tamazight became an official language of Morocco, together with Arabic, and many children now learn to write it in its own ancient alphabet. The teachers face the same problems we do: older speakers who are getting fewer, and young people who prefer the languages they hear on television.

Day 5: After class, the Moroccan teachers took us to a café near the old city, where we drank sweet mint tea for three hours. That café felt like our staff room at home. Everyone talked at once about lesson plans, tired children and how to make grammar fun.

Day 8: We spent two days in a village in the Atlas Mountains, where almost everyone speaks Tamazight at home. The villagers welcomed us into their houses as if we were family. One villager, an old woman, showed me how she weaves, and I showed her photos of my aunt's rugs. The red rock and dry hills look so much like home. Our guide told me that this part of Morocco lies only a little south of our latitude. Nearly the same latitude, the same sky, and yet a world away.

Day 10: Today I rode a camel into the desert. My camel was named Bob, and he complained loudly the whole way. Tyler, I know you will laugh.

Tyler's reply: Hahaha! Mom on a camel! Please send a photo!

Sharon's reply: Photo attached. Bob is not smiling.

Tyler's reply: Hahaha, neither are you.

Day 11: Last night we slept in a tent in the desert. After sunset, one light in the western sky was brighter than all the others. Our guide said it was Venus, the planet that people in many languages call the evening star or the morning star, depending on when it appears. I lay awake and watched Venus sink toward the dunes. I thought about how every nation has its own name for that light, and how many of those names could be lost.

Day 14: Flying home tomorrow. Here is what I learned: we are not alone. Small languages everywhere are fighting the same fight, and we can help each other. We have already planned an online meeting next month.

Questions:
What happened to Sharon's luggage?
It stayed in Paris and arrived the next day.
What problems do the Tamazight teachers share with Sharon?
They have fewer older speakers, and young people prefer other languages.
How did the villagers treat the visitors?
They welcomed them into their houses as if they were family.
Where does that part of Morocco lie, compared with Sharon's home?
It lies only a little south of her home's latitude.
What did Sharon see in the western sky after sunset?
She saw Venus, which many languages call the evening star or the morning star.
